title: Dynamics and characteristics of misinformation related to earthquake predictions on Twitter
screen_reason: Content analysis of a keyword-defined Twitter corpus on earthquake predictions: the paper reports the number and share of tweets classified as misinformation, both in a hand-labeled random sample (698/3,584 = 19.5%, Table 1) and in the full RoBERTa-classified archive (9,857 of 81,862 tweets, Table 2). Both are shares of items in a sample judged against an external ground truth (the state of the art that earthquakes cannot be predicted), i.e. CONTENT prevalence with a denominator.

estimates.measure_type: % of earthquake-prediction/notification tweets in the full keyword corpus classified as misinformation
estimates.value_raw: 9,857 misinformation tweets of 81,862 total classified tweets (Table 2) = 12.0%
estimates.denominator: 81,862 English-language tweets retrieved by the earthquake-prediction keyword query over 1 Mar 2020-31 Mar 2022 (after removing near-duplicates and tweets >350 characters); includes the 36,949 tweets the classifier judged irrelevant
estimates.definition: Tweet classified into the misinformation category, i.e. it claimed to be able to predict a future earthquake
estimates.misinfo_def: "The misinformation category includes all tweets that claimed to be able to predict a future earthquake, according to the state-of-the-art summarized in the recently published Communication  Guide1."
estimates.source_quote: Category # of tweets # of users Tweets/user Misinformation 9857 3804 2.59 Not-misinformation 35,056 4931 7.11 Irrelevant 36,949 27,118 1.36 Total 81,862 34,052 2.40
estimates.page_loc: Table 2 (p. 5); Results, 'Frequency of not-misinformation and misinformation tweets'
estimates.ground_truth_detail: RoBERTa-base fine-tuned on 3,584 hand-labeled tweets; hand labels from two social scientists working on hazard and risk communication in seismology, disagreements resolved by a third person, Cohen's kappa = 0.995; five-fold cross-validation weighted F1 0.845 +/- 0.019, precision 0.85 +/- 0.016, recall 0.85 +/- 0.016
estimates.moderator_quote: "we used the search query [[predict OR forecast OR warn OR updates OR alert] AND [earthquake OR quake OR [seismic AND event] OR seismicity OR shaking OR EQ]]. With this query, we collected 82,129 tweets related to the subject of earthquake prediction, forecasts, and notifications"
estimates.notes: The percentage is not printed; it is an exact part/whole share from the two verbatim Table 2 counts with the same denominator (9,857/81,862 = 12.04%), which R8 permits. I did NOT compute the alternative denominator that excludes the irrelevant tweets (9,857/44,913 = 21.9%), because that would require summing two categories (a cross-category sum, barred by R8). Topic coded science_other (claims about seismology / earthquake prediction); 'other' (natural-hazard/disaster) is the defensible alternative. Year given as the midpoint of the 25-month collection window.

estimates.measure_type: % of randomly sampled earthquake-prediction/notification tweets hand-labeled as misinformation
estimates.denominator: 3,584 randomly selected tweets from the same keyword corpus, hand-labeled into misinformation / not-misinformation / irrelevant (698 + 1,328 + 1,558)
estimates.definition: Tweet hand-labeled into the misinformation category, i.e. it claimed to be able to predict a future earthquake
estimates.misinfo_def: "The misinformation category includes all tweets that claimed to be able to predict a future earthquake, according to the state-of-the-art summarized in the recently published Communication  Guide1."
estimates.source_quote: The final data comprises 81,862 tweets, of which 3584 were manually labeled. The labeled dataset has 698 misinforma- tion tweets, 1328 not-misinformation tweets, and 1558 irrelevant tweets.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two social scientists working on hazard and risk communication in seismology labeled the tweets separately; disagreements resolved by a third person; Cohen's kappa = 0.995
estimates.moderator_quote: "We manually labeled a sample of 4157 tweets into three categories: misinformation, not-misinformation, and irrelevant tweets. The labeling was performed separately by two social scientists working on hazard and risk communication in the field of seismology. The tweets were selected randomly."
estimates.notes: This is the human-coded random subsample of the SAME corpus as the row above, not an independent study: 19.5% is printed verbatim in Table 1 and 698/3,584 reproduces it. Flagged definition_variant=true only as a pooling flag - strictly it is a METHOD variant (human coding vs classifier), not a stricter/broader definition. Do not pool the two rows together; the full-corpus classifier row is the paper's headline number, the hand-labeled row is the gold-standard estimate on a random sample. The two differ (19.5% vs 12.0%) mainly because the classifier assigned proportionally more tweets to 'irrelevant' in the full archive. 4,157 tweets were originally labeled; 3,584 remain after near-duplicate and length preprocessing, and the reported category counts belong to the 3,584.

missed_or_uncertain: 1) URL concentration inside the misinformation group: "over 50% of the tweets linked to three websites, namely emsc-csem.org (21.5%), seismo.info (21.5%), and quakeprediction.com (14.5%)" and "Y ouTube was linked in almost 12.3% of the tweets". Not extracted as CONCENTRATION because R1 requires both conc_group_pct and conc_share_pct: the paper never states how many distinct domains the misinformation tweets linked to, so the top group cannot be expressed as a % of sources. Also, the denominator here is misinformation tweets only. 2) "we found that 79.1% and 84.8% of the tweets in the misinformation group and the not-misinformation group, respectively, contained one or more URLs" and "only about 18-24% of the tweets in each group contained media" - these are shares of tweets containing URLs/media, not shares of misinformation, so no row. 3) Table 2 also gives 3,804 users who posted misinformation out of 34,052 total users; not extracted because the paper never frames this as a prevalence of misinformation-sharing users and the user categories overlap ambiguously with the 'irrelevant' bucket. 4) Event-level counts ("217 general earthquake notifications about the event were published on Twitter. This earthquake sequence led to 25 tweets that claimed to predict the next megathrust earthquake") are one-day counts with no common denominator; per the time-series collapse rule the corpus-level estimate is the representative point. 5) All figures on tweet-level engagement (retweets, likes, replies, sentiment) are means, not shares.

rob.design: Full-archive Twitter academic API v2 keyword search (predict/forecast/warn/updates/alert AND earthquake/quake/seismic event/seismicity/shaking/EQ), English-language, 1 Mar 2020-31 Mar 2022; 82,129 tweets collected, 81,862 retained after removing near-duplicates and tweets over 350 characters. 3,584 randomly selected tweets hand-labeled by two seismology risk-communication social scientists working separately, third-person adjudication, Cohen's kappa = 0.995. A RoBERTa-base model fine-tuned on those labels classified the full corpus (five-fold CV: weighted F1 0.845 +/- 0.019, precision 0.85 +/- 0.016, recall 0.85 +/- 0.016; final model F1 0.8494 on validation). No sampling of users, no response rate (observational platform data); tweets in languages other than English are out of frame.
